chief_complaint: symmetrical brown patches on cheeks after pregnancy
hpi_details: 32-year-old female, 6 months postpartum, presents with symmetric, irregular brown hyperpigmented patches on her cheeks, upper lip, and forehead. Notices it darkens significantly after sun exposure.
ideas: She thinks the dark patches are permanent liver spots brought on by sun damage while her hormones were shifting after childbirth.
concerns: She is worried that the dark patches are permanent and will make her look aged and tired when she returns to her client-facing corporate job next month.
expectations: She hopes to get a prescription skin-lightening cream or a referral for laser therapy to clear the spots before her maternity leave ends.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Melasma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Melasma: Strict sun avoidance, daily sunscreen, hydroquinone cream, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: symmetrical brown patches on cheeks after pregnancy

Key HPI features: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with symmetrical brown patches on cheeks after pregnancy. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Melasma.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Melasma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly enlarging, asymmetric, or dark/variegated pigmented lesion — consider melanoma rather than melasma.
management_principles: Plan for Melasma: Strict sun avoidance, daily sunscreen, hydroquinone cream
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: symmetrical brown patches on cheeks after pregnancy

32-year-old female, 6 months postpartum, presents with symmetric, irregular brown hyperpigmented patches on her cheeks, upper lip, and forehead. Notices it darkens significantly after sun exposure.
reference_soap.objective: Dermatologic exam reveals confluent, reticulated, light-to-dark brown macules and patches on the malar cheeks and central forehead. Wood's lamp examination accentuates the epidermal pigment.
reference_soap.assessment: Melasma (chloasma), likely triggered by recent pregnancy hormones and UV exposure.
reference_soap.plan: Strict photoprotection with broad-spectrum zinc/titanium-based sunscreen daily. Start topical hydroquinone 4% cream nightly. Avoid triggers. Reassure that it may slowly fade over time.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Melasma
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Melasma
Implement evidence-based management plan: Strict sun avoidance, daily sunscreen, hydroquinone cream

teaching.one_liner: Hormonally-triggered hyperpigmentation causing symmetric brown patches on the cheeks, commonly appearing during or after pregnancy.
red_flags: Rapidly enlarging, asymmetric, or dark/variegated pigmented lesion — consider melanoma rather than melasma
New facial hyperpigmentation with other Cushingoid or Addisonian features — evaluate for a secondary endocrine cause

must_ask.say: Are the patches symmetric, on both cheeks?
Did this start during or after a pregnancy, or with a hormonal medication?
Does it get darker with sun exposure?
How long have you had this?

history.answer: I noticed these brownish patches appearing on both of my cheeks after giving birth, and they don't seem to be going away.
They first showed up faintly during the third trimester about six months ago, but since delivering my baby, they have become darker and more noticeable.
They are on both of my cheeks in almost the exact same pattern, and I also have faint patches on my forehead and right above my upper lip.
Whenever I spend time outside in the sun, even for a short walk, the patches darken noticeably and look much more prominent.
They are flat, smooth brown marks with irregular edges. There are no raised bumps, blisters, peeling skin, or scabs.
No, they do not itch, burn, or hurt at all. They just look discolored.
No, they stay there constantly. They never fade or disappear after a few hours like hives do.
I have never had skin pigmentation like this before my pregnancy, and I haven't received any medical treatment for it yet.
I tried using an over-the-counter brightening facial cream for a couple of weeks, but it didn't make any difference at all.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, generalized weakness, or body aches. I feel completely well physically.
No sores, blisters, ulcers, or redness in my mouth, eyes, or genital area.
No, my skin has never blistered or peeled, and I don't have any dark purple spots that stay when pressed.
No swelling of my lips, tongue, or face, and no breathing trouble or lightheadedness.
I haven't started any new prescription medications, antibiotics, pain relievers, or seizure medications.
I haven't changed my cosmetics, skincare products, laundry detergent, or soap, and I don't wear metallic jewelry on my face.
No insect bites, tick exposures, hiking trips, or recent travel anywhere.
I have no history of eczema, asthma, or allergic rhinitis.
No joint pain, swelling, or stiffness, and my nails look completely healthy and normal.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my husband, and I have never had any genital ulcers or sexually transmitted infections.
They definitely started towards the end of my pregnancy and have persisted for the six months since my delivery.
It makes me really self-conscious. I feel like people are staring at my face, and I've been avoiding taking photos with my baby.
I thought maybe my pregnancy hormones reacted with the sun and gave me permanent liver spots.
I'm really worried these blotches will never fade and that I'll look exhausted and unprofessional when I head back to meeting clients at work next month.
I'm hoping you can prescribe a skin-lightening cream or recommend laser treatment that will clear them up before I go back to work.
I don't have any chronic illnesses like thyroid problems, lupus, or high blood pressure.
I had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery six months ago. No other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I am not taking any prescription medications, birth control pills, or herbal supplements right now.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I drink an occasional glass of wine socially, maybe once or twice a month.
I work as an accountant, currently living with my husband and our six-month-old baby.
My mother told me she had similar dark patches on her face after her pregnancies, but no one in my family has had skin cancer.
My periods restarted two months ago and come regularly every 28 days. We use barrier protection, and I am definitely not pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 68 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99%.
Well-nourished, comfortable-appearing female in no acute distress, with symmetric brownish patches across the malar cheeks and forehead.

Confluent, reticulated, light-to-dark brown macules and patches distributed symmetrically across both malar cheeks, upper cutaneous lip, and central forehead; lesions are macular without scale, induration, erythema, or blanching. Remainder of skin examination is clear.
Conjunctivae pink, sclerae anicteric, with no conjunctival injection, lesions, or icterus.
Oral mucosa moist and pink without ulceration, erosions, pigmentation, or mucosal bleeding.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
No joint swelling, redness, or tenderness in bilateral small or large joints; fingernails and toenails appear normal without pitting or discoloration.
